content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's core claim — that 'works' names the deed itself, morally neutral until the governing lawgiver is identified, and that a deed becomes obedience by executing God's command or disobedience when another lawgiver governs it — is directly carried by its cited texts. Exodus 18:20 defines the term where the law is first taught ('the work that they must do' as the third member alongside ordinances taught and a way walked, distinguishing work from the command it executes). Micah 6:16 is nearly a proof-in-miniature: the 'works of the house of Ahab' are deeds that execute the 'statutes of Omri' — the same word 'works' used of deeds commanded by a rival lawgiver, which is exactly the book's mechanism for evil works. Luke 17:7-10 establishes the second half of the entry: even complete obedience earns no wage, which lets the book read Romans 4:4-5 as opposing labor-offered-for-wages rather than opposing obedience, and James 2:21-22 as works enacting faith rather than purchasing anything. This resolves the Paul/James tension with fewer unsupported steps than the alternatives: the evidential-fruit reading must soften James's 'justified by works,' and the New Perspective must confine Romans 4's laborer/wage image to covenant boundary markers, which the wage metaphor itself resists. The strongest counter (works as fruit/evidence of inner condition) agrees that the referent is deeds and disputes only emphasis and mechanism, not the identification; the book's own chapter in fact affirms the evidential function ('by works was faith made perfect'). No supplied text is better explained by a counter-reading than by the book's core.","book_core_identification":"'Works' means deeds as such — not a synonym for obedience or for righteous acts. The word is morally unfixed: the same deed is obedience when it executes God's command and disobedience when another lawgiver governs it; the context, not the word, names the deed's master and whether a wage is claimed for it.","book_secondary_elaborations":["Even complete obedience earns no wage — the servant has only done his duty (Luke 17:7-10), so Romans 4 opposes labor-offered-for-wages, not obedience itself","Romans 4 and James 2 use the same word for two different transactions: a laborer's work presented for wages versus Abraham's work as faith made visible and perfected","Works are 'commandment-shaped' and can therefore be 'kept' (Ps 111:7; Rev 2:26), pairing God's works with His commandments as two halves of one line","Works enact faith rather than rename it: faith without works is dead because a faith that never acts never becomes faithfulness"],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream evidential-fruit reading (Responses A–C primary meaning): 'works' are the outward deeds that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition — good works being the fruit of genuine faith, grace, and regeneration; evil works being the fruit of the flesh, unbelief, or darkness. A tree is known by its fruit; works reveal the heart and are the basis of judgment because they manifest it, while salvation is by grace through faith and not of works (Eph 2:8-10; Jas 2:14-26; Matt 7:16-20; Gal 5:19-23; Rev 20:12-13).","counter_core_identification":"'Works' are deeds or conduct functioning as the visible fruit and evidence of a person's inner spiritual state — good works flowing from faith and grace, evil works from the flesh and unbelief.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"A genuinely rival core would have to claim that 'works' is intrinsically valenced — that the word itself denotes righteous obedience (or, in Paul's polemic, denotes self-righteous effort as such), so that a deed's moral character is fixed in the term rather than determined by which lawgiver commands it and whether a wage is claimed. On that denial, 'works of the house of Ahab' and 'the work that they must do' could not share one neutral term whose master is supplied by context.","counter_case":["Matthew 7:16-20 and Matthew 5:16 present deeds as fruit by which the inner tree is known and God is glorified — an evidential function the book's neutral-deed definition does not foreground","Ephesians 2:8-10 and Titus 3:5 set works against grace in salvation, supporting a reading in which 'works' in Paul's polemic carries the fixed negative sense of human effort offered for standing","Galatians 5:19-23 pairs 'works of the flesh' against 'fruit of the Spirit,' suggesting works are expressions of an inner nature rather than deeds awaiting a lawgiver's assignment","Revelation 20:12-13 grounds judgment in works because they manifest the heart, the standard evidential framing","The New Perspective alternative reads Paul's 'works of the law' as Jewish covenant boundary markers, giving Romans 3-4 an ethnic-inclusion referent rather than a wage-transaction referent"],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Micah 6:16 is decisive for the book's mechanism: 'the works of the house of Ahab' are deeds executing 'the statutes of Omri' — the word 'works' applied to command-execution under a rival lawgiver, which the fruit-of-inner-state framing does not specifically predict","Exodus 18:20 defines 'work' at the law's first teaching as the deed to be done, formally distinct from the ordinances taught and the way walked — supporting 'deed, not a synonym for obedience'","Luke 17:7-10 plus Romans 4:4-5 yields a clean reconciliation of Paul and James: Paul excludes the wage-claim, not obedience (since even complete obedience earns no wage), while James's works enact faith — the evidential reading must instead manage James 2:21's 'justified by works' as loose speech, and the NPP must fit Romans 4's laborer/wage image to boundary markers it does not naturally describe","Psalm 111:7 and Revelation 2:26 ('keepeth my works') explain why works can be 'kept' — works are commandment-shaped deeds — a linguistic detail the generic fruit reading leaves unexplained","The neutral-deed core accounts for both poles (good works and evil works, God's works and Ahab's works) with a single definition plus a context variable, rather than treating Paul's negative uses and James's positive uses as different senses of the word"],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["The fruit/evidence framing more directly captures Matthew 7:16-20's tree-and-fruit logic and Galatians 5:19's 'works of the flesh' as manifestations of nature","It matches the dominant homiletic and confessional usage, so it explains the term's reception history","It keeps Ephesians 2:8-10's grace/works antithesis simple without needing the wage-claim distinction"],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Micah 6:16 — 'works of the house of Ahab' as deeds executing the statutes of a rival lawgiver, the book's mechanism stated in the text itself","Exodus 18:20 — 'work' defined at the law's first teaching as the deed to be done, distinct from the ordinances and the way","Luke 17:7-10 — complete obedience earns no wage, severing obedience from wage-claiming and enabling the Romans 4 reading","Romans 4:4-5 with James 2:21-22 — the same word in two transactions: labor for wages versus faith made visible and perfect","Psalm 111:7 — God's works and God's commandments as parallel halves of one line, showing works as commandment-shaped deeds"],"unresolved_objections":["The book's entry does not itself articulate the evidential function of works (deeds as fruit revealing the heart, Matt 7:16-20), though the proving chapter's treatment of faith 'made perfect' by works substantially absorbs it","Psalm 111:7's parallelism is suggestive rather than demonstrative for the works/commandments pairing","The New Perspective reading of 'works of the law' as covenant boundary markers in Romans/Galatians is not directly engaged, though Romans 4's laborer/wage imagery independently favors the book's transactional reading","Whether Paul's polemical uses (Rom 9:32; 11:6) ever harden 'works' into a fixed negative sense, rather than remaining context-assigned, is not fully adjudicated by the cited texts"],"confidence":"high"}
